chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who attained wealth from the work of the Banu Umayya, and he gives charity from it, maintains kinship ties from it, and performs Hajj so that what he had earned may be forgiven for him, and he says, 'Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds.'

So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: 'An error does not expiate an error, but a good deed removes an error.' Then he said: 'If he mixed the permissible with the prohibited, so they all became mixed, and the permissible is no longer distinguished from the prohibited, then there is no problem.'

key_terms.بَنِي أُمَيَّةَ: The Clan of Umayya, often cited as a source of doubtful wealth

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on spending mixed wealth where the halal and haram portions are indistinguishable?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) refutes the notion that sins expiate sins, clarifying that only good deeds erase them, while addressing the practical issue of mixed permissible and prohibited wealth. He establishes the principle of *khalat* (mixing), ruling that if the halal and haram portions become indistinguishable, the entire amount is treated as permissible for use. This ruling provides significant relief for those dealing with the vast, often ambiguous earnings of the Umayyad administration, emphasizing ease in financial transactions when certainty is lost.
